segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul, a slave of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, set apart for the good news of God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy scriptures,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: concerning his Son, who came from the seed of David according to the flesh,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who was appointed Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by resurrection from the dead: Jesus Christ our Lord,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: through whom we received grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith among all the Gentiles for the sake of his name,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and among them you also are called to belong to Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To all who are in Rome, loved by God, called to be holy ones: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is being proclaimed throughout the whole world.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God, whom I serve with my spirit in the good news of his Son, is my witness how unceasingly I make mention of you

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: always in my prayers, asking that somehow, now at last, by God’s will, the way may be opened for me to come to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I long to see you, so that I may share with you some spiritual gift to strengthen you;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that is, to be encouraged together among you through each other’s faith, yours and mine.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I do not want you to be unaware, brothers and sisters, that I have often planned to come to you, and have been prevented until now, so that I might have some fruit among you also, just as among the rest of the Gentiles.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To Greeks and to barbarians, to the wise and to the foolish, I am a debtor;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so for my part I am eager to proclaim the good news to you also who are in Rome.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I am not ashamed of the good news, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, as it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “But the righteous one will live by faith.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of people who suppress the truth in unrighteousness,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because what can be known about God is plain among them, for God has made it plain to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For ever since the creation of the world his unseen qualities, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood through the things he has made, so that they are without excuse,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their reasonings, and their senseless heart was darkened.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Claiming to be wise, they became fools,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and exchanged the glory of the imperishable God for the likeness of an image of a perishable human being, and of birds and four-footed animals and creeping things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore God handed them over in the desires of their hearts to impurity, to the dishonouring of their bodies among themselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They exchanged the truth of God for the lie, and worshipped and served the creation rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this reason God handed them over to dishonourable passions. For their females exchanged natural relations for those contrary to nature,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and likewise the males also, abandoning natural relations with the female, were inflamed with craving for one another, males committing shameful acts with males and receiving in themselves the repayment that was due for their error.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And just as they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God handed them over to an unfit mind, to do what is not proper,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: filled as they are with every kind of unrighteousness, wickedness, greed and malice; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit and spite. They are gossips,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: slanderers, God-haters, insolent, arrogant, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: senseless, faithless, heartless, merciless.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Though they know full well God’s righteous decree, that those who practise such things deserve death, they not only do them but also approve of those who practise them.

notes.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a person owned by another, not a hired servant. Paul's first readers in Rome, a city full of slaves and freed slaves, would have heard it that way. The Septuagint also uses the word for honoured figures such as Moses and David as ‘slaves of the Lord’, so it carries dignity as well as total belonging. Many translations soften it to ‘servant’; a growing number now print ‘slave’.

The Greek word meant an announcement of good news, such as a victory or a ruler's accession, and the Septuagint uses the related verb for announcing God's saving reign. ‘Gospel’ once meant exactly this but is now heard mainly as a religious term or a kind of book. Most translations keep ‘gospel’ in Paul; several modern ones use ‘good news’.

Elsewhere in the period the verb means to fix, determine or appoint, and that is how it is used in the rest of the New Testament. ‘Declared’ became traditional partly to avoid suggesting that Jesus only became God's Son at the resurrection. Most commentators now accept ‘appointed’ or ‘designated’, taking ‘in power’ with ‘Son of God’: the one who was already Son was installed as Son-in-power by the resurrection.

The Greek phrase can mean the obedience that springs from faith, the obedience that consists in faith, or simply faithful obedience. The literal rendering is kept because the Greek does not decide between them and scholars remain divided. The same phrase returns at the close of the letter (16:26).

Greek has one word here for ‘nations’ and ‘Gentiles’; in the plural it regularly means the non-Jewish peoples. ‘Among all the nations’ is therefore equally possible in this verse. ‘Gentiles’ is used because Paul goes on to describe his mission as directed to non-Jews (verse 13).

The word is the ordinary adjective ‘holy’ used as a noun for all members of the community, as people set apart for God; it echoes the Septuagint's language for Israel. ‘Saints’ now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue, which is not what is meant. Many translations keep ‘saints’; others use ‘God's holy people’.

The Greek masculine plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of siblings or fellow members, and Paul's letters were read aloud to congregations that included women (several are greeted by name in chapter 16). ‘Brothers’ alone now sounds as if only men are addressed. Older translations have ‘brethren’ or ‘brothers’; many recent ones have ‘brothers and sisters’.

In Greek usage the word meant anyone who did not speak Greek or share Greek culture; it could be condescending but did not in itself mean ‘savage’. ‘Greeks and barbarians’ was a stock way of saying all humanity as seen from the Greek side, just as ‘Jew and Greek’ in verse 16 is the same division seen from the Jewish side.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous/just, righteousness/justice, justify. The phrase itself is disputed: it may mean God's own rightness shown in acting to save and set things right, as often in the Psalms and Isaiah, or a right standing that comes from God as a gift. ‘Righteousness’ is kept as the traditional and majority rendering; some scholars prefer ‘justice’ or ‘covenant faithfulness’. ‘Unrighteousness’ in verses 18 and 29 is the negative of the same word.

The phrase is compressed and disputed. It may be an emphatic way of saying ‘by faith from start to finish’, or it may mean from God's faithfulness to human faith, since the Greek word covers both faith and faithfulness. ‘By faith’ in the quotation that follows (Habakkuk 2:4) is the same Greek phrase as ‘from faith’ here. The quotation can also be read as ‘the one who is righteous by faith will live’.

Paul does not use the ordinary words for ‘women’ and ‘men’ in verses 26–27 but ‘females’ and ‘males’, the terms of the Greek version of Genesis 1:27 (‘male and female he made them’). The choice fits a passage that argues from creation, and the rendering keeps it visible. Most translations have ‘women’ and ‘men’.

notes.traditional: reprobate mind / debased mind / depraved mind
notes.note: Paul plays on two related words: they did not ‘approve’ God after testing, so God gave them over to a mind that ‘fails the test’. ‘See fit’ and ‘unfit’ reproduce the echo. The traditional renderings give the sense of a mind that has failed but lose the wordplay.

In earlier Greek the word is passive, ‘hated by the gods’, and some scholars read it so here (‘hateful to God’). Because every other item in the list is a vice and not a consequence, most translators take it actively, as here.

This translation normally renders the word ‘righteous requirement’ or ‘righteous act’. Here it refers not to something God requires but to his verdict that such conduct deserves death, so ‘decree’ is used. ‘Righteous’ is retained to show the link with ‘righteousness’ in verse 17.

Very frequent, and ‘gospel’ versus ‘good news’ (with the verb εὐαγγελίζομαι) must be decided once or the English will alternate between chapters.
The plural address occurs throughout the letters and Acts, and translators divide between ‘brothers’ and ‘brothers and sisters’.
A key Pauline term rendered variously as ‘flesh’, ‘human nature’, ‘sinful nature’ or ‘physical descent’; it needs a single policy by sense.
The negative of the δικαιοσύνη family; translators vary between ‘unrighteousness’, ‘injustice’ and ‘wickedness’, and the link to the register's ‘righteousness’ is lost if it varies.
